analysis.one_liner: Redirects new workers' Social Security payroll taxes into personal bank-held retirement accounts and halves their guaranteed benefits.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past committee: introduced by one Republican with zero cosponsors, it received a single hearing in October 1994 and died when the Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: For workers new to Social Security starting in 1995, the bill would wipe out the 6.2% employee Social Security tax and instead require employers to send that same money into a personal retirement account at a bank the worker chooses. Self-employed people could do the same. In exchange, those workers' eventual Social Security checks would be cut to half of the normal benefit, with the account intended to make up the difference.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers entering the workforce after 1994 (and self-employed people who elect in) would own an individual retirement account funded by the money that currently goes to their Social Security tax. The account would be theirs, inheritable by a surviving spouse, and withdrawals at retirement age would be tax-free. Employers would see their own Social Security tax rate drop slightly, from 6.2% to 6.06%. Banks would gain a new stream of mandatory deposits, since every account must be administered by a bank.

how_it_helps.text: Eligible employees would pay 0% in employee Social Security tax; the same amount would instead be deducted from wages and deposited into their own account within 10 business days.

The account is a true individual retirement account: the worker owns it, a surviving widow or divorced spouse inherits the balance, and qualified distributions at retirement age are excluded from income tax.
Employers' own Social Security tax rate would drop from 6.2% to 6.06%, and plans without employer contributions would be exempt from most ERISA benefit-plan rules.
Employers would have to run the payroll deduction plan at their own expense, so workers would not pay account-setup or payroll fees to their employer.

analysis.who_pays: Participants' guaranteed Social Security benefits would be cut to 50% of the standard formula, moving retirement risk from a government guarantee to their own account's performance. The Social Security trust fund would lose the employee share of payroll revenue while still owing full benefits to everyone already in the system. Employers would bear the cost of administering the deduction plan without compensation, with civil penalties up to $5,000 (or $100 per employee) for failing to set up a plan and up to 50% of deducted amounts for late deposits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Future retirees, the trust fund, employers

drawbacks.text: A participant's Social Security benefit would be 50% of the normal formula (scaled between 50% and 90% for workers who affirmatively elected in, based on work quarters earned before 1995), replacing a guaranteed, inflation-adjusted pension with an account exposed to market results.

The Social Security trust fund would lose the employee share of contributions while current and near-retirement beneficiaries are still owed full benefits, worsening the program's financing during the transition.

Every account must be administered by a bank, channeling a mandatory stream of worker contributions through one industry; workers taking money out early would face a 50% penalty, five times the standard 10% early-withdrawal penalty on ordinary IRAs.
Employers would bear uncompensated administrative duties backed by stiff civil penalties for missed deductions or late deposits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Workers would own real, inheritable accounts funded by money now going to a tax, and employers would get a small tax cut. But the trade is risky and uneven: participants would give up half of a guaranteed benefit in exchange for an account whose value depends on markets, the transition would drain the trust fund while obligations continue, and the design funnels every worker's contribution through banks. Early withdrawals would carry an unusually harsh 50% penalty. It is a genuine structural trade-off, not a free lunch, and it was offered with no cosponsors and no fiscal analysis in the record.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in subcommittees of the Ways and Means and Education and Labor committees, got one hearing in October 1994, and died when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, without ever coming to a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Thomas of California introduced the bill on February 3, 1994, with no cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Ways and Means and Education and Labor committees, then to their Social Security and Labor-Management Relations subcommittees in February and March 1994.
The only recorded action after that was a committee hearing held on October 4, 1994; no markup or floor vote ever occurred.
The bill expired with the 103rd Congress in January 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Traditional Social Security was left unchanged: no worker's guaranteed benefit was cut and no payroll contributions were diverted. Banks never gained the mandated account system. Nothing about the outcome disadvantaged workers, though supporters of personal accounts gained nothing either.

for.name: Rep. William M. Thomas
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it jointly to the Ways and Means and Education and Labor committees; attracted no cosponsors.

against.name: Rep. Sam Gibbons
against.role: Chairman, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup after the bill's referral; the Ways and Means Social Security subcommittee held one hearing and the bill went no further.

against.name: Rep. William Ford
against.role: Chairman, House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup after the bill's referral to his committee and its Labor-Management Relations subcommittee.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken. The sole sponsor was a Republican and zero members of either party cosponsored, while the Democratic chairs of both referred committees took the bill no further than one hearing.

industries.note: Every account must be an IRA administered or issued by a bank, so the bill would route a mandatory stream of contributions from every new worker through banks indefinitely. Banks would gain captive deposits while the cheaper public alternative (the traditional benefit) is cut in half.

Employers' Social Security tax rate would drop from 6.2% to 6.06%, but they would have to operate the payroll deduction plan at their own expense, facing civil penalties up to $5,000 or $100 per employee and up to 50% of deducted amounts for late deposits.
